Statement 
(a) and (b) As per reports received from Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and 
National Bank for Agriculture and Ru ral Development (NABARD), it is not 
correct to say that most of the coopera tive Banks in the country are weak. Of 
the 2087 urban cooperative Banks in the country as on 31st October, 2001 only 
262 are classified as weak, constituting 12.6% of the total number of urban 
cooperative Banks. Similarly, the statutory inspection of State Cooperative 
Banks (SCBs) and District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) have revealed 
that as on 30th June, 2001,7 SCBs out of 30 and 141 DCCBs out of 369 having 
negative networth can only be classifed as weak. 
(c) and (d) A Task Force headed by Shri Jagdish Capoor constituted by 
Government to study the cooperative credit system has indicated that weakness 
in the cooperative credit structure is primarily due to dual control of RBI and 
State Governments, limited resources, dependence on higher financing agencies, 
lack of skilled manpower, viability probl ems and inadequate spread, extreme 
politicalisation/bureaucratic interference, rising cost and lack of professional 
management, etc. 
(e) and (0 It is not correct to say that the norms/guidelines issued by RBI 
are flouted by «ost of the Banks. RBI/NABARD take appropriate action 
wherever any of these Banks are found to be not complying with the provisions 
of Banking Regulation Act or guidelines issued by them.

Out of 2084 Urban Cooperative Banks that are presently operating in the

Hijacking of Alliance Airlines Mumbai-Delhi Flight 
* 24.   SHRINILOTPALBASU: 
SHRIS. NIRAIKULATHAN: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state:   . 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government had gone on record confirming 
the hijacking of an Alliance Air late night flight from Mumbai to Delhi; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it subsequently turned out to be a case of false alarm; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(e) the system which was in place at the time of the incident and the 
details thereof and the points at which this system was breached; and 
(0 whether any accountability has been fixed? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) to (f) On 3.10.2001 at 23.22 hours an anonymous telephone call 
was received about the imminent hij acking of Alliance Air flight CD-7444 
operating on Mumbai-Delhi sector. This message was received when the flight 
was already airborne. The message was conveyed to the aircraft with instructions 
to take necessary precautionary measur es. However, due to some misunder-
standing, the pilot-in-command concluded that the plane had been hijacked and 
activated the hijack signal at around 00.12 hrs. The aircraft landed at IGI Airport 
at 00.50 hrs. 
Based on the message received from the aircraft, information regarding 
the reported hijack was shared with all concerned. As per the systems in place, 
necessary measures were initiated on ground for handling the unlawful interfer-
ence in aviation activity. 
ATC, Delhi was constantly in touch with the aircraft, and efforts were 
made to elicit relevant information, including in regard to the number of 
hijackers, their position etc. It was subsequently decided to send the National 
Security Guard Commandoes through the cockpit window. It was only after 
these commandoes later went into the cabin, and segregated the two suspected 
passengers, that it became clear that th ere were no armed hijackers on the 
aeroplane, and that a false alarm had been given. 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2001 ] 
A high level Committee was constituted under the Chairmanship of Special 
Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs to examine in totality the situation arising 
out of the chain of events triggered by an anonymous telephone call regarding 
the imminent hijacking of flight No. CD-7444 operating on Mumbai-Delhi sector. 
The Committee has since submitted its report. In the meantime Alliance Air has 
placed the entire, crew of the flight off the flying duties.

* 37.   SHRI K.M. KHAN:

THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) and (b) Even though no comprehensive study has been made so 
far to assess the overall impact of the recent terrorists attack on the U.S. cities on 
the aviation industry, international Air Transport Association (IATA) has 
estimated the loss to be around USD 7 billion (Rs. 35,000 crores) on international 
33 

RAJYASABHA [20 November, 2001] 
services worldwide. There has been seve re crisis of confid ence in air travel 
amongst the consumers. This has led to a reduction of about 17% in passenger 
traffic in September itself as compared to previous year. The passenger load 
factor fell from 78% in August to 69% in September. LATA has also estimated 
that member airlines have laid off 1,20,000 employees (7% of their total staff). 
Additionally, aircraft manufacturers have announced lay off on nearly 56,000 
employees. Airlines have also resorted to capacity cuts between 10% and 20% 
on different sectors. Insurance companies have also limited 3rd party liability 
cover in respect of war, terrorist and other allied activities to USD 1 bilion and 
imposed additional war risk insurance charge at the rate of USD 1.25 per passenger. 
As far as India is concerned, there has been large scale cancellation of 
travel plan by tourists and business travellers from the US and Western Europe 
leading to decline in traffic post September 2001. Air India was forced to cancel 
its flights from the US due to the closure of US air space for 4 days suffering a 
loss of Rs.8.5 to 10 crores. Due to declining international traffic, United Airlines 
has discontinued operation to/from India, North West Airlines has discontinued 
its operation to Delhi, Gulf Air has w ithdrawn 3 frequences between Bahrain 
and Mumbai, Swiss Air has withdrawn its operations, SAS has decided to 
discontinue operation w.e.f. February 2001, Canada 3000 has deferred its plan 
for operation and Air India has curtailed flights to UK/USA, Japan, Singapore, 
Hong Kong and Muscat. 
It is true that aviation market is down now, but there are inherent strength 
of Air India and therefore, the tragic events of 11th September 2001 are unlikely 
to have any adverse impact on the disinvestment of Air India in the long term. 
In the short term airlines including Air India have reduced their capacity 
to match the reduced demand. Government of India has provided indemnity to 
the tune of the USD 500 million to Air India which is equal to the shortfall in the 
3rd party cover required and the same available in the market till 30.11.2001. This 
cover which was valid only till 12.10.2001 has been extended by the Government 
till 30.11.2001. However, following security/safety measures have been taken to 
improve the confidence of the. consumers and to ensure fool proof security of 
operation: 
CO    Anti sabotage checks of all aircraft. 
(ii)    Access control of the aircraft both at the passenger doors and cargo 
holds.

HUSSAIN): (a) and (b)The net loss suffered by Air India during the year 2000-

currencies; and (vi) increase in interest expenditure on working capital loans.

for agricultural products for developing countries through reduction of export

and Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) measures, moratorium of two years on 
non-violation complaints under Trade-Related aspects of Intellectual Property 
Rights (TRIPS) Agreement, investigating authorities to examine with special

and members to offer cooperation and assistance including furnishing information 
about export value when the customs administration of an importing Member

ing countries as well as anti-dumping problems; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINSTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) German Chancellor Mr. Gerhard 
Schroeder during his recent visit to Indi a in October, 2001 held discussions 
with Indian leaders on various issues  including on trade liberalisaion. The 
German Chancellor in his discussions did not specifically seek India's support 
for the new trade negotiations at Doha. However at a seminar on Indo-German 
Economic Relations; Looking Ahead jointly organised by CII & FICCI at New 
Delhi, the German Chancellor stated, inter alia, that India's concerns on 
implementation are legitimate but this should not stop us from having the next 
round of negotiation. 
(b) The Fourth Ministerial Confer ence of the WTO was held from 
November 9 to 14th, 2001 at Doha , Qatar. The Conference adopted the 
Ministerial Declaration on 14th November containing decisions on a number of 
issues. India actively participated in the Ministerial Conference and a significant 
number of issues of interest to India were included in the Ministerial Declaration. 
These include important issues like greater market access for agricultural products 
for developing countries through reduction of export subsidies and trade 
distorting domestic support given by developed countries, food security and 
rural development concerns of developing countries in agriculture negotiations, 
addressing the issue related to extension of protection of geographical indications 
to products other than wines and spirits, protection of traditional knowledge &

folklore, Public Health and access to medicines, clarification and improvement of 
disciplines relating to anti-dumping and subsidies and countervailing measures, 
special and differential treatment for developing countries and negotiations on 
makret access for non-agricultural products aimed at elimination of non-tariff 
barriers and tariff peaks and tariff escalations. India strongly opposed the 
inclusion of non-trade social issues like labour within the ambit of WTO. The 
Declaration recognises that the International Labour Organisation (ILO) is the 
appropriate forum to address the issue of core labour standards. The Ministerial 
Conference decided to initiate negotiation only on few items of agenda of 
Committee on Trade and Environment (CTE) while the remaining items have 
been referred to the study process until the Fifth Ministerial Conference. On the 
Singapore issues relating to Investment, Competition Policy, Trade Facilitation 
and Transparency in Government Proc urement, the Mini sterial Conference 
decided to launch negotiations after the Sth Session of Ministerial Conference 
only on the basis of decisions to be taken at that session by "Explicit Consensus". 
(c) The Doha Ministerial Conference has adopted Decisions on a number 
of Implemenation Issues and Concerns of the developing countries. The decisions 
which confer significant benefit to India include longer time frame of six months for 
complinace with new Sanitary and Phyto-Sanitary (SPS) and Technical Barriers to 
Trade (TBT) measures, moratorium of two years on non-violation complaints 
under Trade Related Aspects or Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) Agreement, 
investigating authorities to examine with special care for initiation of back to back 
antidumping investigation within 365 days, and members to offer cooperation and 
assistance including furnishing information about export value when the customs 
adminstration of an importing Member has reasonable grounds to doubt the truth or 
accuracy of the declared value. The outstanding implementation issues would be 
addressed as an integral part of the Work Programme of the WTO decided by the 
Doha Ministerial Conference.

Statement 
Recommendations / Observations of the High Powered Committee on E- 
Commerce and Taxation 
1. The Committee desires the consideration of neutrality of taxation of e-
commerce vis-a-vis traditional commerce, ensuring integrity of the direct tax bases 
and working for international consensus keeping the national interest in view. 
2. The effect of e-commerce on the concept of permanent establishment (PE) and 
characterisation of income in respect of payments in cross border transactions have 
been examined by the Committee. The Committee is of the view that the concept 
of PE needs to be abandoned. Under the existing principles of international taxation 
the server of a non-resident enterprise, hosting its Website, would constitute a PE 
if the server is at the disposal of the enterprise, and remains at a fixed place for a 
period of time and performs the core business functions of the enterprise. 
However, this does not lead to certainty of taxation in view of the possibility of 
use of minor servers. It also results in shifting of equilibrium in revenue sharing in 
favor of countries of residence as against countries of source, because very little 
income would be attributable to such a stand-alone server. 
3. The issues regarding characterisation of income through cross border payments 
have been examined with reference to the 28 categories of transactions 
considered by the Tax Advisory Group (TAG) of Organisation 
90 

[20 November, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). The Committee's views 
differ from those of the OECD in regard to a number of these categories. The 
Committee has recommended that a view should be taken in regard to each of the 
28 categories to ensure uniformity of approach by different Assessing Officers. It 
has also recommended regular monitoring of new emerging categories of 
transactions as a continuous process. 
4. With regard to enforcement the Committee is of the view that the extent of e-
commerce, particularly online e-commerce is nominal at present and is not likely 
to be significant in near future. However, the enforcement challenges will 
arise once the problems in delivery and payment mechanism are sorted out. 
A number or recommendations have been made to prepare the Income-tax 
administration to meet these challenges. 
5. Finally, the Committee has pointed out areas in which taxpayer services can be 
improved through the use of Internet. 
The Report is now available on the web site of the Ministry of Finance: http:/ 
/www.finmin.nic.in for comments/opinion from the public.

addition, the rule removes many Indian and Pakistani entities from the Entity 
List. The license review policy for items classified as EAR 99 (Items that are 
subject to the EAR, but are not listed on the Commerce Control List) has also 
been revised and the policy now presumes approval for all Indian and Pakistani-
listed entities. Items on the Commerce Control List (CCL) will be considered on 
a case-by-case basis. The entitites which remain on the Entity List are as follows: 
Bharat Dynamics Limited (1 entity), DRDO (4 entities), DAE (3 entities and all 
nuclear reactor activity related entities,  including power plants) and ISRO (8 
entities).

221. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have made an indepth-study and analysis of the

be made in the growth model worked out to take the sluggish economy out of 
its present depression? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATTL): (a) and (b)The Mckinsey Global Institute, 
in collaboration with Mckinsey's India Office have conducted a study on the 
Indian economy entitled India: The Growth Imperative Understanding the 
barriers to Rapid Growth and Employment Creation. Its major findings is that 
India can achieve a growth rate of 10 per cent per annum. Besides, the study has 
identified 3 main categories of barriers, viz., product market barriers, land market 
barriers and Government ownership that constrain India's GDP growth. With a 
view to dismantle the three main barriers the study has suggested 13 point 
reform programme. The suggestions made by various organisations/ institutions 
and othes are considered keeping in view the trends in the economy and 
Government's broad policy objectives. With a view to acheive higher growth 
the braod strategy outlines in the Budget for 2001-2002 has emphasised 
speeding up of agricultural sector reforms and better management of the food 
economy; intensification of infrastructure investment, continued reform in the 
financial sector and capital markets, and deepening of structural reforms through 
removal of remaining controls constraining economy activity; human 
development through better educational opportunities and programmes of social 
security; stringent expenditure control of non productive expenditure, 
acceleration of the privatisation process and restructuring of public enterprises 
and; revenue enhancement through widening of the tax base and administration 
of a fair and equitable tax regime. The strategy is expected to have a favourable 
impact on overall growth.

Self-Sufficiency in Hydro-Carbon Sector 
270. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) what steps are Government taking towards achieving self-sufficiency in the 
Hydro-Carbon Sector; 
(b) what percentage of our requirements of Crude Oil and Natural Gas is 
produced annually in the country; and 
(c) the details of the production for the last three years, item-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS (SHRISANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) Given the increasing demand for 
petroleum products and the current level of import dependence of around 70 percent, it 
is difficult to envisage self-sufficiency in the near future. However, several important 
steps have been taken to increase oil and gas production, which include the 
following steps: 
0) to improve the recovery factor from existing major fields by 
implementing Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) Improved Oil 
Recovery (IOR) schemes; in particular Oil and Natural Gas 
Corporation Limited (ONGC) has taken up 15 fields for this purpose at an 
estimated investment of Rs. 10,000 crore, which would .also help in 
accelerating oil production from these fields. 
(ii) to increase exploration efforts through the New Exploration Licensing 
Policy (NELP). Under the first round of NELP, Production Sharing Contracts 
(PSCs) have been signed for 24 blocks in which works are in progress. 
Additionally, under the second round of NELP, PSCs have been signed 
on 17.7.2001 for 23 blocks. 
(iii) to attract technology and investment, PSCs for 9 discovered fields, 8 in 
Gujarat and 1 in Assam, were signed on 23.2.2001 with consortia of Indian 
and foreign companies. 
(iv) to explore in new areas, especially in deep water and difficult frontier areas, as 
also explore in the deeper layers of the producing fields. 
152 

[20 November, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) to develop faster the newly discovered fields and to step up the use of new

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATIBUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Water being a State subject,

has to be enacted by the States/Union Territories. However, in 1970 the Union

groundwater level in many parts of the country which have adverse effects on 
various aspects including environment and forests. Water being a State subject, 
action to augment water supplies and repl enishing of groundwater is to be 
taken by the concerned State Government The Union Government supplements 
the efforts made by the State Governments by providing technical and financial 
assistance in this regard.

JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has more than five crore disabled people; 
(b) whether over 98 percent of them have little or no access to education 
*The sitting of the Rajya Sabha on Monday, the 19th November, 2001

and scholarships are given only to deserving disabled students with limited 
means; and 
(c) if so, the steps being taken by Government to provide a helping hand 
for the disabled persons in view of their great success in every field? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (DR. 
SATYA NARAYAN JATTYA): (a) to (c) As per the sample survey conducted by 
the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) in 1991, approximately 5% of 
the population is estimated to be affected by some kind of disability. A large 
proportion of these persons are in the older age group and not within the age 
group for formal education. 
With a view to ensuring that all children includung those with disabilities 
get access to education, the governme nt has launched the Sarwa Shiksha 
Abhiyan. Through this, several options are available to children with disabilities 
for pursuing their education in inclusive schools, integrated schools, through 
non- formal system, National Open School and through institutions for special 
education run by government and voluntary organizations. The scheme of 
Integrated Education for Disabled Ch ildren (IEDC) provides for additional 
support by way of developing resource rooms in schools, teaching aids, assistive 
devices and transportation for the children. Many of the State Governments 
also provide scholarships and other support to children with disabilities to 
encourage them to pursue their education. To facilitate students with disability 
in pursuing education at the higher level, the Persons with Disabilities Act 
provides for reservation of 3% seats in admissions in educational institutions 
run or aided by government. 
Besides, rehabilitation services and vocational training are provided 
through Government run institutions and voluntary organizations. For the 
economic empowerment of persons with disabilities and to encourage their 
self-employment, they are supported through Swamajayanti Gram Swarozgar 
Yojana (SGSY) and loan programmes of financial institutions and banks.

Introduction of Genes from one Organism to Another 
28. SHRI C. O. POULOSE: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the vectors used for introducing genes 
from one organism to another to make a Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) are 
highly infectious and virulent biological agents; 
(b) if so, whether the risks of the use of virulent vectors for engineering novel 
life form have been assessed; and 
215 

 
RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2001 ] 
(c) if not, how is it possible to create a bio-safety network since their use 
for bio-terrorism becomes easier as they spread commercially around the world? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Genes can be moved from one species to another 
unrelated species by using the techniques of genetic engineering. A vector 
made up of a host compatible promoter, a gene of interest and a terminator 
sequence can be used to insert the transgene into the host by several 
established transformation techniques. Once a transformed host is made and 
the transgene is in the right orientation within the chromosome of the host 
organism, it will express. If the products of the transgene are not toxic to the 
host, the host would survive. If the products are toxic to unrelated organisms, 
the transformed host can dangerous as it would multiply under favourable 
conditions and in the process would produce large quantities of toxins. 
Therefore, a case by case analysis is required before any genetically modified 
organism is introducd in to the environment. A v ector is not necessarily 
virulent or infectious. 
Genetic transformation can take place in nature but the probability of 
such transformation is extremely low. Moreover, the transformed host has to 
survive under natural conditions, which is usually found to be extremely 
difficult. 
Indian System of regulation is transparent in dealing with genetically 
modified organisms. All experiments are to pass through a three tier regulatory 
process where there is vigilance from th e Government at each stage to keep a 
watch on what is being developed or used locally. The three tier system 
comprise creation of an Institutional Bio-Safety Committee at the Institute/ 
Company where research work is carried out or where transgenic materials are 
developed: the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation is a Central 
Committee housed at the Department of Biotechnology, while the Genetic 
Engineering Approval Committee which is the Statutory Body to deal with all 
aspects of genetically modified organisms and products thereof is in the 
Ministry of Environment & Forests. Wherever materials do not enter through 
the three tier system, the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 can act heavily 
on the offender as such acts are considered  to be criminal in nature and they 
attract punitive actions.

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P.

Statement-I 
Salient features of Centrally Sponsored Health Scheme 
1. National Family Welfare Programmes: The programme is fully 
voluntary and the effort is to provide services on one hand and to encourage 
the citizens by information, education and communication on the other hand. 
Reproductive Child Health, supply of  contraceptives, compensation for 
sterlisation and IUD insertion, salary contingency, rent etc. of infrastructure 
set-up, area specific projects, research institutes and maintenance of transport 
are different compo- nents of the programme. 
2. National Anti-Malaria Programme: The strategy for malaria control 
includes early case detection and prompt treatment, selective vector control, 
promotion of personal protection methods, containment of epidemics and IEC 
towards personal protection and community participation. 
3. National Leprosy Eradication Programme: The programme is 
implemented through district leprosy societies. Funds and anti-leprosy drugs 
are provided to all the district leprosy societies for providing MDT service free 
of cost to all the needy patients. 
4. National T.B. Control Programme: To detect as many T.B. cases as 
possible and to effectively treat them so  as to make the infectious cases non-
infectious. Another feature of the progr amme is to integrate the programme 
with primary health care infrastructure. 435 million population of the country 
is presently covered under the programme. 
5. National Blindness Control Programme: Development of eye care 
infrastructure, training of personnel, assistance to NGOs, free cataract surgery, 
assistance to eye banks and school ey e screening programme are the various 
activities of this programme. 
224 

[20 November, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
6. National AIDS Control Programme: Reducing the spread of HIV among 
high risk groups, preventive intervention for the general population through 
IEC and awareness campaigns, provision of voluntary testing facilities, safe 
blood transfusion services and promoting collaboration amongst public, private 
and voluntary sector are the major components of this programme. 
7. Drug Inspectorate Staff in States/UTs: Under this scheme 50 percent of 
the salary of the additional staff required was to be borne by States/UTs with the 
balance 50% of the requirement to be borne by the Centre. As many States/UTs 
did not agree to these conditions the centrally sponsored scheme could not 
take off. 
Statement-II 
Funding pattern of Centrally Sponsored Health Schemes 
1. National Family Welfare Programme: This is a 100% Centrally 
Sponsored programme. Funds are released to State Governments for meeting 
out the liability of infrastructure set-up across the country based on the 
number of centres sanctioned and estab lished for each State upto 1980. This 
includes the salary alongwith rent for building, contingency, stipend and fuel. 
Norms have been fixed for giving grants-in-aid for all items other than 
salary. 
2. National Anti-Malaria Programme: Expenditure is shared on 50:50 
basis between the States and Central Government. However, in respect of North 
Eastern States 100% central assistance is being provided w.e.f. 1.12.1994. 
Enhanced Malaria Control Programme is also under implementation with World 
Bank Assistance in 100 districts of 8 States and 19 identified urban areas where 
assistance is provided in terms of insecticides, drugs, rapid diagnostics, bednets, 
etc. besides cash grants to district malaria control societies for operational 
expenses. 
3. National Leprosy Eradication Programme: Funds are provided as 100% 
grant to States/UTs according to physical  targets set up by the States and 
endemicity of the disease. 
4. National T.B. Control Programme: 100% requirements of Anti-T.B. 
drugs is met by the Centre w.e.f. April, 1997. Anti-T.B. Drugs for all T.B. cases 
in RNTCP areas and for sputum positive cases in non RNTCP areas are supplied 
by centre to the districts as commodity grant. For procurement of anti-TB.

drugs for sputum negative cases in non RNTCP areas, cash assistance as grant-
in-aid is released to the State Governments. In RNTCP areas, funds are released 
to districtT.B. control societies for implementation of revised strategy on 100% 
central support basis. 
5. National Blindness Control Programme: Funds are released to the 
States on the basis of physical targets and utilisation of funds allocated. 
6. National AIDS Control Programme: Funds are allocated to the State 
AIDS Control Societies based on the action plans submitted by them.

Health which was participated by Secretaries of Home and Health from various States and 
Union Territories. They have taken stock of the preparedness to face any situation 
including availability of drugs and all the states have been asked to strengthen their 
public health system to handle the situation effectively. In this context a detailed list

Research along with signs and symptoms, likely method of dissemination, 
incubation period, lethality and the availability of vaccines, anti-microbial therapy 
and treatment has been circulated to all the States and Union Territories and Central 
Govt. Hospitals in order to take precautionary steps such as earmarking of maximum

with special reference to anthrax was ci rculated in October, 2001 to all the 
concerned health authorities in different states and Union Territories. The issue 
also covered the guidelines to the followed during biological war/terrorism 
and effective handling of suspicious envelops/package. 
(iii) Guidelines for packaging, transportation of clinical specimens and 
processing protocol in laboratories were circulated to all the Medical Colleges 
in the country; 
(iv) A meeting on chemical and bio-terrorism was organized on 29th 
October by the Department of Health which was participated by the 
Secretaries of Home & Health. Director of Health Services from various States/ 
Union Territories. The representatives from the States informed the preparatory 
measures taken by them and assured availability of drugs in adequate quantity 
to tackle any situation as per their disaster management plan.

identified as the nodal agency to for investigations of any specimen suspected

National Population Policy 
53. SHRIRAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) what concrete steps Government have taken to stablize the unregulated 
growth of population to give incentives to persons with small families and to 
undertake half-yearly or yearly survey of increase/decrease in population after 
adoption of a comprehensive National Population Policy, State-wise; 
(b) whether any campaign has been launched, so far against the practice of 
female foeticide in order to arrest the adverse sex ratio in certain States; and 
(c) by when the Pre-Natal Diagnostics Act, 1994 will be amended/brought 
before Parliament for approval? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) The following are some of the initiatives taken during the last two 
years on the issue of containing the growth of population and expediting the pace of 
implementation of National-Family Welfare Program: 
Stabilizing population 
For the first time in independent India, a comprehensive National 
Population Policy has been adopted by the Government with the 
objective of improving the quality of life of the citizens, by reaching out 
to them with an enhanced package of services and supplies, that will 
inter-alia, serve to stabilize the unregulated growth of population. 
National Commission on Population has been constituted directly 
under the chairmanship of Prime Minister with Chief Ministers of all 
States/ UTs, demographers, non-government organizations and public 
health professionals as members to advise in operationalising the 
National Population Policy. 
An Empowered Action Group has been constituted under the 
chairmanship of the Union Health and Family Welfare Minister for ' 
focussed attention on improving the coverage and outreach of services 
in the eight States of Uttar Prad esh, Uttranchal, Bihar, Jharkhand, 
Rajasthan, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh and Chhatisgarh, involving voluntary 
associations, community organizations and Panchayati Raj institutions 
in this national effort. 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2001 ] 
Series of consultations have been held with all stakeholders i.e. the 
State Health and Family Welfare Ministers, State Secretaries, 
professional medical associations and medical experts, NGOs, media 
persons, Corporate sector and ci vil society for implementation of 
the National Population Policy, 2000. 
In order to arrest the adverse sex ratio, an intensive campaign has 
been launched against the practice of female foeticide through the 
mass media, print and electronic, as well as through the voluntary 
organizations for stricter enforcement of the Law. The Pre-Natal 
Diagnostics Techniques Act, 1994 is being amended as well to 
cover the new emerging technologi es and for ensuring effective 
implementation of the Act. 
Male participation in the programme has increased mainfold with 
the growing popularity of No  Scalpel Vasectomy—a much-
improved method. 
Upgradation of health infrastructure 
The Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojna has provided in the two .     
years 2000-2001 and 2001-02 central allocation of Rs. 809 crores for 
the maintenance and upkeep of primary health infrastructure in rural 
India. 
. Area specific projects have been taken up for strengthening primary 
health care services in the States  of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, 
Orissa, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Kerala under Integrated Population 
Development (IPD) Project supported by UNFPA, for slums in cities/ 
towns in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and West Bengal 
in World Bank supported IPPVIII project, in Assam and Karnataka 
IPPIX project, in 33 district of U.P. under IFPS project supported 
by USAID, in Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and demographically 
deficient areas under various prog rammes with the assistance of 
DANIDA, DFID and World Bank. 
Norms for payment for items like rent, contigencies, stipend etc. for 
family welfare infrastructure units which were fixed in 1970s and 
80s have been revised. 
In order to strengthen the availability of health staff steps like 
development of cadre of Nurse Midwives in public and private 
256 

[20 November, 2001] RAJYASABHA 
sector, contractual appointments of ANMs, Public Health Nurses, 
and Laboratory Technicians have taken. Private Doctors and 
Anesthetists are being engaged on payment per visit basis. 
Integrated service delivery: Reproductive health 
• Immunization is key to health of children by reducing infant 
mortality. RCH outreach services such as immunization, ante and 
post natal check ups, information and counselling, as well as 
contraceptive services are being provided. This scheme which 
covered 50 district last year, has been extended during the current 
year to 101 additional districts. 
• In an effort to supplement existing interventions seeking to expand 
outreach and coverage, a series of "Parivar Kalyan and Swasthya 
Melas" have been held all over  die country including Mathura, 
Delhi, Lucknow, Kargil, Patna, Badal, Perambur, Sultanpur (U.P.) 
and Ghazipur (U.P). Many more are being planned. 
• RCH Camps are also periodically organised at primary health centres 
for providing integrated services to the rural population, especially 
women and children, in remote and under-services to the rural 
population, especially women and children, in remote and under-
served areas. The scheme, which was started in 101 district last year, 
has now been extended to 77 additional districts in the current 
year. 
• The programme for training of traditional birth attendants (Dais), 
with provision of kits, has been introduced in 142 districts with a 
record of less than 30% safe deliveries. 
• Resources and skills of the Indian Systems of Medicine are also 
being utilized in the RCH Program. Effective Ayurved and Unani 
medicines for common ailments of women and children are being 
supplied to Sub Centres/institutions in 7 States, in particular. 
• Private-public partnership through the NGO movement has been 
net-worked in 412 districts. 
• Polio on its way out 
• Intensive Pulse Polio campaigns have helped in reducing the 
number of confirmed polio cases from 1126 in 1999 to 265 in year 
257 

RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2001 ] 
2000 and to 112 this year. Transmission of the vims is now virtually 
confined to a few districts of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. During the 
current year, in addition to strengthening the routine immunization 
programme, two National Immunization Days will be organised all 
over the country on December 2, 2001 and January 20, 2002. One 
Sub-National Immunization Day has been held on October 14, 
2001, in the States of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Delhi and West Bengal. 
With vigorous implementation of the programme and intensified 
efforts in Uttar Pradesh and Bi har, we are confident that "Zero 
incidence of Polio" will be reached by next year.   . 
New Programme on Newborn Care 
• Neonatal mortality comprises over 50% of the infant mortality in 
the country. To serve the lives of the Newborn, a special Newborn 
care programme was launched in 60 district of the country in 
collaboration with the National Neonatalogy Forum last year. This 
programme will be extended to other backward district this year. 
Another initiative being encouraged by the Government for proper 
newborn care is training and empowering of community level 
newborn care workers, specially through NGOs. 
• The Pilot project for testing the feasibility of introducing Hepatitis-
B vacine in immunization programme in slums of 15 metropolitan 
cities and 32 selected rural districts has been approved by the 
Government. 
(b) and (c) After the Census 2001 figures were available, letters have been 
addressed to the Chief Ministers of all States/UTs to give focussed attention to 
the issue of adverse sex ratio. Chief Secretaries of all the States/UTs have also 
been addressed recently for following up on implementation of various provi-
sions of the Pre-natal Diagnostic Technique Act The States/UTs have been 
advised to mount an effective awareness compaign to make the public and 
service providers aware of the provisions of the Act. The States/UTs have also 
been advised to provide protection to social activists and Non-Governmental 
Organizations giving information or filing complaints of violation of provisions 
of the Act. 
Workshops/Seminars are being organised at State/district level, to create 
awareness about the provisions of the Act Voluntary Organisations are also 
being involved to carry out projects regarding creating awareness about the 
258 

[20 November, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
provisions of the Act. Grant-in-aid has also been released to two NGOs viz. 
Orissa Voluntary Health Association and Voluntary Health Association of India, 
New Delhi to conduct seminars and workshops and other Information, Educa-
tion and Communication (IEC) activities in the States of Orissa, Punjab, Madhya 
Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu. 
National Level Non-Governmental Or ganisations have been requested 
to take up projects for generating awareness about the provisions of the Act, 
among doctor/clinics law enforcing authorities and public at large. In December, 
2000 the Department of Family Welfare has written letters to 82 Mother NGOs 
to direct the field NGOs to generate w ithin their jurisdiction, awareness and 
public opinion against the mal-practice of selective abortion. The co-operation 
of the NGOs has also been requested in listing and enumerating, within their 
jurisdiction, the name and address of premises where the Medical Termination 
of Pregnancy (MTP) is being performed, with a view to detect registered/ 
unregistered clinics. 
The Technical Sub-Committee of the Central Supervisory Board of the 
Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 
1994 has suggested necessary amendments to be made in the Act in view of the 
emerging technologies including separation of X and Y chromosome leading 
to selection of sex of unborn child before conception as well as name and pre-
amble of the existing Act The Central Supervisory Board of the Pre-natal 
Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994, in its 
meeting held on 18th October, 2001 has given is consent to the amendment 
suggested by the Technical Sub-Committee. The proposed Bill for amendments 
may be brought in the current session of Parliament.

Meeting with the Indian Pharmaceutical Industry 
55. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a delegation from the Indian Pharmaceutical Industry 
called on him some time back in Mumbai in connection with the difficulties being 
experienced by the Industry for carrying out research and experimentation on 
animals; 
(b) if so, the details of the points raised by the delegation; and 
(c) the details of assurance given by him to the delegation and the follow up 
action, if any, taken to fulfill the assurance? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The issue was informally raised. However, no formal 
representation was given. The delegation raised the point that the research based 
pharmaceutical industry has to invest heavily for 'new drug discovery research*. 
Approval of any new molecule for human studies requires generation of adequate pre 
clinical safety data on different species of animals. This is also a statutory requirement 
under Schedule 'Y' of Drugs and Cosmetic Rules, 1945. Further in view of the new IPR 
Regime under TRIPS agreement Le. product patent from 2005, there is an increasing 
need for Indian firms to discover and develop new drugs. 
However, the rules prescribed for animal experimentation and procedure 
prescribed by CPCSEA (Committee for the purpose of Control and Supervision of 
experiments and Animals) makes it very difficult for research based industry to use 
larger animals like Beagle Dogs and Monkey. Being a statutory 
260 

[20 November, 20011 RAJYASABHA 
requirement companies have to conduct such studies through private contract 
research organizations abroad which is very costly. 
Pharmaceutical Industry desired to remove such impediments by 
modifying the Breeding of and Experiments on Animals (Control and 
Supervision) Rules. 
The matter is receiving the attention of the Government. 
Bill for monitoring guidelines in medical research 
56. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government intend to bring forward a Bill 
during the Winter Session of Parliament making provision for monitoring 
guidelines in medical research; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) whether Government would take care to ensure that the proposed 
legislation does not contain too many restrictions which would curb the already 
limited value of medical research currently carried on in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) There is a proposal to make a comprehensive legislation 
on the ethical guidelines on Bio-Medical Research on human subjects. The 
need for uniform ethical guidelines for research on human has acquired urgency 
as the critical issues in the areas of biogenetic research involving human subjects 
have become acute. The legislation on the ethical guidelines is proposed with 
a view to ensure compliance by scientific community for protection of basic 
human rights and safety to research participants.

74.   SHRIK. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
WiU the Minister of INFORMATIONAND BROADCASTING be pleased to state:

morality; 
(c) whether any guidelines have been issued in this regard; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) Government of India approved the DTH policy 
on 2.11.2000 and guidelines were issued on 15.3.2001. 
(b) to (d) The salient features of the guidelines are as follows:— 
i) Eligibility Criteria: 
• Applicant Company to be an Indian Company registered under Indian 
Companies Act, 1956. 
• Total foreign equity holding including FDI / NRI / OCB / FU in the 
applicant company not to exceed 49%. 
• FDI component of the foreign equity not to exceed 20%. 
• The quantum represented by the portion of the paid up equity share capital 
to the total issued equity capital of the Indian promoter company held or 
controlled by the foreign investors through FDI / NRI / OCB investment 
shall form part of the FDI limit of 20%. 
• The applicant company must have Indian management Control with 
majority representatives on the board as well as the CEO of the 
company being a resident Indian. 
• Broadcasting companies and / or cable network companies shall not be 
eligible to own more than 20% of the total equity of Applicant Company 
at any time during the licence period. Similarly, the applicant company 
not to have more than 20% equity share in a broadcasting and / or cable 
network company. 
275 

RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2001] 
ii) Number of licensees: 
• There will be no restrictions on th e total number of DTH licenses and 
these will be issued to any person who fulfils the necessary terms and 
conditions and subject to the secur ity and technical clearances by 
the appropriate authorities of the Govt. 
iii) Period of Licence: 
• Licence will be valid for a period of 10 years and is not transferable 
without prior approval of licensor. 
iv) Basic conditions I obligations: 
The licence will be subject to terms and conditions contained in the 
agreement which inter-alia, provides that 
• licensee shall adhere to programme and advertisement code, 
• set up earth stations in India, give non-discriminatory access to 
various contents providers, 
• carry channels of Prasar Bharati on most favourable terms, 
• maintain recordings of programmes and advertisements for a period of 90 
days. 
v) Protection of Consumer Interest: 
• The licensee shall use the open Architecture (non-proprietary) Set Top 
Box, which will ensure technical compatibility and interoperability 
among different DTH service providers, and shall have such 
specifications as laid down by the Government from time to time. 
• The Conditional Access System (CAS) to be used will be 
compatible with open architecture Set Top Box. 
• The licensee shall ensure subscribers' interest through the 
subscriber management system, which is efficient, responsive and has 
accurate billing and collection system. 
276 

[20 November, 2001] RAJYASABHA 
• The licensee shall adhere to regulation, which may be laid down 
in the interest of consumer such as pricing of bouquet(s) or tier(s) 
of channel etc. 
vi) National Security Concerns: 
• Immediate termination of licence may be done if facility or service 
is used for anti-national activities. 
* Access to all facilities to licensors or its authorized representative 
to be provided by licensee. 
• Right of Government to take over me entire service in the interest of 
national security. 
• Requirement that all foreign personnel deployed shall obtain 
security clearance. 
vii) Procedure for application and grant of licences: 
• Application to be submitted to the Secretary, Ministry of I&B, in 
triplicate, in the prescribed proforma. 
• On the basis of information furnished in the application form, if the 
applicant is found eligible for setting up of DTH platform in India, 
the application will be subjected to security clearance by the 
Ministry of Home Affairs and for clearance of satellite use by the 
Department of Space. 
• After these clearances the applicant would be required to make non-
refundable entry fee of Rs. 10 crore to Ministry of I&B and obtain 
from Wireless Planning and Coordination (WPC) Wing of Ministry of 
Communications, S ACFA clearance. 
• After this clearance is obtained, the applicant would be required 
to furnish a bank guarantee for Rs. 40 crores and sign a licensing 
agreement with the Ministry of I&B as per prescribed proforma. 
277 

RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2001 ] 
Within one month from the date of the signing the licensing 
agreement with the Ministry of I&B, the licensee shall apply to WPC 
for seeking Wireless Operational Licence for establishment, 
maintenance and operation of DTH platform. 
The licensee shall commission DTH within one year of SACFA clearance. 
The licensee shall pay an annual fee equivalent to 10% of its gross 
revenue within one month of the end of every financial year to the 
government in addition to licence fee and royalty for the spectrum 
used. 
For any additional value — added service, separate licence to be obtained

96. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of SHIPPING

(a) whether Government are aware that current share of Inland Waterway s 
Transport (IWT) is merely 1.5 billion tonnes Km. as compared to total inland 
Cargo of over 1,000 billion tonnes Km. inspite of the fact that India has an 
extensive network of 15,000 Km. waterways; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps taken/proposed to be taken by Government for upgradation 
of infrastructure in the sectQr and increase the IWT? 
293 

RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2001 ] 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING (SHRI VED PRAKASH GOYAL): 
(a) to (c) According to National Transport Policy Committee Report (1980) 
India has about 14,500 Km of navigable inland waterways out of which about 
5700 Km are suitable for navigation by  mechanized craft. Three waterways 
namely the Ganga from Haldia to Allahabad, the Brahmaputra from Dhubri to 
Sadiya and West Coast Canal from Kottapuram to Kollam along with 
Udyogmandal and Champakara canals totaling 2176 km in length have been 
dec'ared as National Waterways. Basic level infrastructural facilities for shipping 
and navigation are being provided in these waterways. Besides there is cargo 
movement in Goa and Mumbai inland waterways. Shifts of cargo from developed 
modes viz. rail and road to IWT would take place only after the inland waterways 
are developed with adequate infrastructure namely fairway, terminals and night 
navigational aids, and cargo vessels are operated by public or private carriers 
in a substantial manner. Actions for providing these facilities, including private 
sector participa- tion in IWT, are in hand. 
Techno economic feasibility studies for assessing the potential/ 
navigability have been conducted on more waterways. With a view to giving 
an impetus to IWT sector and to encourage private sector participation in IWT 
infrastructure development and ownership and operation of inland vessels, the 
Government has approved an IWT policy in January, 2001. Several policy 
measures and incentives to private sector have been included in this Policy.

Statement 
The National Population Policy, 2000 
The immediate objective of the National Population Policy is to address the 
unmet needs of contraception, health infrastructure, health personnel and to provide 
integrated service delivery for basic reproductive and child health care. The medium 
term objective is to bring the total fertility rates to replacement level by 2010, through 
vigorous implementation of inter sectoral operational strategies. The long-term 
objective is to achieve a stable population by 2045, at a level consistent with the 
requirements of sustainable economic growth, social development and 
environmental protection. 
In pursuance of these objectives, the following National Socio-
Demographic Goals are to be achieved in each case by for 2010 are formulated: 
(1) Address the unmet needs for basic reproductive and child health 
services, supplies and infrastructure. 
312 

[20 November, 2001] RAJYASABHA 
(2) Make school education upto age 14 free and compulsory, and reduce 
drop outs at primary and secondary school levels to below 20 per cent 
for both boys and girls. 
(3) Reduce infant mortality rate to below 30 per 1000 live births. 
(4) Reduce maternal mortality ratio to below 100 per 100,000 live births. 
(5) Achieve universal immunization of children against all vaccine 
preventable diseases. 
(6) Promote delayed marriage for girls, not earlier than age 18 and 
preferably after 20 years of age. 
(7) Achieve 80 percent institutional deliveries and 100 per cent deliveries by 
trained persons. 
(8) Achieve universal access to information/counseling, and services for 
fertility regulation and contraception with a wide basket of choices. 
(?) Achieve 100 percent registration of births, deaths, marriage and 
pregnancy. 
(10) Contain the spread of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) and 
promote greater integration between the management of 
Reproductive Trace Infection (RT I) and Sexually Transmitted 
Infractions (SIT) and the National AIDS Control Organisation. 
(11) Prevent and control communicable diseases. 
• (12) Integrate Indian System of Medicines (ISM) in the provision of 
reproductive and child health se rvices, and in reaching out to 
households. 
(13) Promote vigorously the small family to achieve replacement levels 
ofTFR. 
(14) Bring about convergence in implementation of related social sector 
programmes so that family we lfare becomes a people centred 
programme. 
To achieve the above goals, the NPP, 2000 envisages constitution of the 
following bodies: 
313 

RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2001 ] 
(i)   National Commission on Population 
(ii) State/UT Commission on Population 
The National Commission on Population was constituted on 11th May, 2000 
under the chairmanship of the Prime Minister to oversee and review the 
implementation of the Policy. The first meeting of the Commission was held on 
22nd July, 2000. 
State/UT Population Commissions have been constituted in Andhra 
Pradesh, Aninachal Pradesh, Assam, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, J&K, Kerala 
Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim, 
Tamil Nadu, A&N Islands and Lakshadweep. Many other States have informed that 
they are in the process of constituting this Body. 
At the first meeting of the National Commission on Population, Prime 
Minister has announced the formation of an Empowered Action Group, in the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, in particular for paying focussed attention 
to those States with deficient national socio-demographic indices. The 
Empowered Action Group will provide support in respect of design and monitoring 
of projects and programmes for reproductive and child health, as well as IEC 
campaigns. 
The National Population Policy, 2000 has identified the immediate 
objectives as meeting the unmet n eeds for contraception, health care 
infrastructure and trained health personnel and to provide integrated service 
delivery, with the following interventions: 
(i) Strengthen, community health centres, primary health centres and sub-
centres; 
(ii)  Augment skills of health personnel and health care providers; 
(iii) Bring about convergence in the implementation of related social sector 
programme so that the family welfare programme becomes a people 
centred programme; 
(iv) Integrate package of essential services at village and household levels by 
extending basic reproductive and child health care through mobile clinics 
and Counselling services; 
(v) Explore the possibility of accrediting private medical practitioners 
314 

[20 November, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
and assigning them to defined beneficary groups to provide these 
services and revive the system of licensed medical practitioners, who 
could provide specified clinical services. 
National Population Policy, 2000 inter-alia enumerates the following 
promotional and motivational measures for adoption of the small family 
norms:—  
(1) Panchayats and Zila Pari shads will be rewarded and honoured for 
exemplary performance in universalising the small family norm, 
achieving reductions in infant mortality and birth rates and promoting 
literacy with completion of primary schooling. 
(2) The Balika Samridhi Yojana run by the Department of Women and Child 
Development, to promote survival and care of the girl child, will continue. 
A cash incentive of Rs. 500 is awarded at the birth of the girl child of birth 
order 1 or 2. 
(3) Maternity Benefit Scheme run by the Department of Rural 
Development will continue. A cash incentive of Rs. 500 is awarded to 
mothers who have their first child after 19 years of age, for birth of the first 
or second child only. Disbursement of the cash award will in future be 
linked to compliance with ante-natal check up, institutional delivery by 
trained birth attendant, registration of birth and BCG immunisation. 
(4) A Family Welfare linked health Insurance Plan will be established. 
Couples below the poverty line, who undergo sterilisation with not 
more than two living children, would become eligible (along with 
children) for health insurance (for hospitalisation) not exceeding Rs. 
5000, and a personal accident insurance cover for the spouse 
undergoing sterilisation. 
(5) Couples below the poverty line, who marry after the legal age of 
marriage, register the marriage, have their first child after the mother 
reaches the age of 21, accept the small family norms, and adopt a 
terminal method after birth of the second child, will be rewarded. 
(6) A revolving fund will be set up for income-generating activities by 
village-level staff help groups, who provide community-level health 
care services.

(7) Creches and childcare centres will be opened in rural and urban slums. 
This will facilitate and promote participation of women in paid 
employment 
(8) A wider, affordable choice of contraceptives will be made accessible at 
diverse delivery points, with counselling services to enable acceptors 
to exercise voluntary and informed consent. 
(9) Facilities for safe abortion will be strengthened and expanded. 
 
(10) Products and services will be made affordable through innovative social 
marketing schemes. 
(11) Local entrepreneures at village levels will be provided soft loans and

(12) Increased vocational training schemes for girls, leading to self-

SHRI N.K. PREMCHANDRAN (Kerala): Mr. Chairman, I am raising a 
matter of urgent national importance conc erning the national security of our 
country. 
The mining and mineral separation of sand on the coastal area of 
Kerala is exclusively conducted by tw o public sector undertakings, i.e. the 
Indians Rare Earths Ltd. (IRE) Chavar a and the Kerala Mineral and Metals 
Ltd. (KMM), Chavara. Both these un dertakings are having advanced modern 
technology, high productivity and are running profitably. 
Now, the Government of Kerala has processed mining lease 
applications of some private companies and forwarded them to the 
Government of India for approval on the basis of the resolution of the 
Department of Atomic Energy dated 6 th October, 1998 declaring the policy of 
exploitation of beach sand minerals. 
By virtue of this policy resolution, IRE had invited global tenders for 
mining and mineral separation in the year 1998 and subsequently it was 
withdrawn considering the public interest. 
But the new move initiated by the Government of Kerala to grant 
mining lease to private companies to mine beach sand minerals and to 
separate minerals will endanger our country's internal security since strategic 
elements like thorium are extracted fr om these minerals. It would also 
destabilise the very existence of our mo st prestigious and profitable public 
sector undertakings like IRE and KMML, Kollam. Hence, I urge upon the 
Government of India, t he Department of Mines and the Department of Atomic 
Energy not to grant approval for mining by private companies. There is also a 
simultaneous move to have a joint venture in the process of mining and 
mineral separation by IRE, with a private company. The said joint venture 
proposal is totally adverse to the interest s of IRE. The proposal is likely to be 
decided at the meeting of the IRE's Board of Directors on 28 th November, 
2001. Hence, I urge upon the Government of India to intervene in this matter 
immediately and to stop all the procee dings in connection with the joint 
venture proposal of IRE.

GOVERNMENT BILL 
THE EXPLOSIVE SUBSTANCES (AMENDMENT) BILL, 1999 
 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO):  Mr. Chairman, Sir, I move: 
"That     the     Bill     further     to     amend     the     Explosive 
Substances Act, 1908, be taken into consideration". 
Sir, as the hon. Members are aware, the Explosive Substances 
(Amendment) Bill, 1998, was passed by the Lok Sabha on 17 th, December, 
1998, but before the Bill could be tak en up in this august House, the 12 th Lok 
Sabha was dissolved and the Bill, accord ingly, lapsed. For the information of 
this august House, I would like to mention that the incidents of bomb 
explosions have been on the increase in th e recent past in various parts of 
the country, particularly in the States  of Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Tamil 
Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and the North-East, and there have been immense 
loss of life and property. The frequent  occurrence of such incidents has 
adversely affected the security environment in the country and has created a 
serious law and order situation. Enquir ies have revealed that the terrorists 
and anti-social elements are increasingly using sophisticated 
362 

[20 November, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
explosives like RDX (Research De velopment Explosive), PETN (Penta 
Erythritol Tetra Nitrate) and other simi lar types of explosive substances in 
carrying out their nefarious activities. These improved variety of explosives 
are difficult to detect in the normal course and are far more lethal and 
damaging than conventional explosives. 
Since the existing Explosive Substances Act, 1908, makes no 
distinction between offences involving the use of conventional types of 
explosives, compared with the improv ed and sophisticated types of lethal 
explosives, a review of the provisions of the existing Act was conducted by 
the Ministry of Home Affairs so as to make its provisions more stringent in 
respect of explosions carried with the use of sophisticated explosives like 
RDX and PETN. 
The Bill was introduced in this august House on 23.12.1999 and was 
considered by the Parliamentary Sta ndfng Committee on Ministry of Home 
Affairs at its meeting held  on 8.2.2000. In their re port presented to the House 
on 15.3.2000, the Committee had made  certain recommendations for 
consideration of the Government. These recommendations have been 
considered, in consultation with the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company 
Affairs and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. I am happy to inform that 
the recommendations of the Committee have been, by and large, accepted by 
the Government; and, based on the recommendations of the Committee, 
certain amendments are proposed to be made to the pending Bill, as per my 
notice dated 6th November, 2001; these are the following:- (1) Clause 2 (b) of 
the Bill is proposed to be amended to enable Central 'Government to include 
any new special category 'explosive' subs tance by issue of a notification. It is 
proposed to recast the wordings of Se ctions 3,4 and 5 of the Act so as to 
prescribe minimum punishment for various offences and to enhance the level 
of punishment under these Sections of the Act to the level of death penalty 
and rigorous imprisonment for life, in case where RDX, PETN and other similar 
types of explosives or combination thereof, and remote control devices are 
used to cause such explosions. (3) It is proposed to add a new clause in the 
Bill so as to provide for the exercise of  powers of sanction of prosecution by 
the District Magistrate in the States/Uni on Territories, in place of the Central 
Government. 
With the above, I request that  the Explosiva Substances 
(Amendment) Bill, 1999, be considered and passed by this august House. 
The question was proposed.

SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU  (Pondicherry): Mr.vlce-
Chairman, Sir, I support this Bill. My learned friend, Shri Shirodkar, 
said that the words "unlawfully and maliciously" should be removed 
from clauses 3, 4 and 5 of the Bill. I am constrained to differ from his 
opinion on this count. As far as these clauses are concerned, the 
possession of RDX and other explosive substances are punishable 
under these provisions of the Bill. Suppose RDX that belongs to a 
third party is kept in my land. It is deemed that I am in possession of 
the RDX and I can be straightaway prosecuted under these 
provisions, if these words "unlaw fully and maliciously" are removed. 
Taking into account what is meant  by possession the framers of the 
Act have incorporated the words "unlawfully and maliciously" in

3, 4 and 5 of the Bill. The words "unlawfully and maliciously" are there 
in sections 3, 4 and 5 of the original Act of 1908. 
My learned friend, Shri Ramachandran Pillai, said that the 
words "maliciously and intentionally" should be incorporated in section 
6 of the Act. I submit with great respect that it is not necessary 
because section 6 relates only to the abetment of an offence. The 
main offences are under sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act. If any person 
abets, he is liable to prosecution under section 6 of the Act. Since the 
words "unlawfully and maliciously" are there in the main sections 3, 4 
and 5. there is no necessity to mention those words in section 6 of the 
Act. That is why they have been omitted in section 6. Suppose I 
committed the murder of a person and I knowingly committed it. If any 
person abets the same, automatically  the main provisions of the 
relevant Act are attracted. So, it is not necessary to include those 
words in section 6 of the Act. 
My next submission before this august House is that the 
Standing Committee on Home Affairs has recommended the inclusion 
of rigorous imprisonment in clauses 3 and 4 of the Bill. Clause 3 says, 
"with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description 
for a term which may extend to ten years". Clause 4 says, "with 
imprisonment for life". Clause 5 says, "with rigorous imprisonment for 
life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten 
years". Life imprisonment means rigorous imprisonment. We should 
have either omitted the words "rigorous imprisonment" in clause 5 or 
included those words in clauses 3 and 4 of the Bill. Though the 
Standing Committee on Home Affairs specifically recommended the 
inclusion of "rigorous imprisonment" in clauses 3 and 4 of the Bill, 
those words have not been include d. Otherwise, they have no 
meaning at all. 
As far as the amendments are concerned, we are not 
departing too much from the original Act of 1908. In the original 
sections 3 and 4, there is a provision for deportation of a person for 
life to another country. Section 3 specifically mentions about 
transportation for life. In section 4 also there is a provision for 
transportation for a term which ma y extend up to 20 years. Under the 
Indian Penal Code presently there is no transportation for life. In order 
to mitigate that, imprisonment for life has been incorporated. Actually, 
they are reducing the punishment  provided by the 1908 Act to life 
imprisonment. There is only one section where the death sentence is 
mentioned. In all other sections it is only life imprisonment. Over a 
period of four years 2,000 explos ions took place and 1,200 people 
died in those

SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR  RAO: Sir. the case has

The hon. Member, Shri Ahluwalia mentioned about the inclusion of 
Anthrax in this category. Since it is not an explosive substance, it cannot be 
included. However, the suggestions c an be taken into consideration. Shri 
Pillai mentioned certain important aspects of  the Bill. Sir, this Bill is only for 
inclusion of certain explosive substances and for creating a special category of 
these substances like research developme nt explosive, pent a erythritol tetra 
nitrate. This was discussed in t he Committee and the Committee, after 
thorough examination and deliberati on, has made certain recommendations. 
The suggestion made by the hon. Member is not acceptable because this is 
just a small amendment; the original Act is already there and provision for 
rigorous punishment like life imprison ment and so on is already there. 
Sections 5 and 6 are already there.  Nothing has been changed. The only 
thing that has been done is only to keep pace with the escalated crime 
scenario in the country; certain substances which were not there have now 
been included. Otherwise, no Section has be en touched at all. Sir, there is no 
intention to interfere with the existi ng scheme of Sections 3, 4, and 5. The 
proposal is only to make the provisions more stringent, by providing for higher 
punishment in the case of explosives which are very lethal in nature. 
Sir, the last point which was mentio ned by the hon. Member is that 
by utilising this clause, innocent persons will be punished, and mere 
possession of any explosive material ma y lead to punishment by death. That 
was the apprehension of the hon. Me mber. Sir, clause 5 deals with the 
possession or control of explosives under circumstances which give rise to the 
reasonable suspicion regarding the lawfulness of the object behind such 
possession or control. The lawful possession, use, manufacture, sale, 
transport, import and export of explosives are matters regulated under a 
different Act. The Explosives Act of 1884 and the rules made thereunder are

there. A person can use a small dynamite for doing certain canal work, but he 
cannot use any explosiv e substance like RDX or any improvised explosive 
devices like this. Therefore, definitely, it does not attract it. There are separate 
laws for it. If he is an innocent person, then, no harm would be done to him. 
He can use those kind of explosives. There is a separate Explosives Act in 
this regard. It can be dealt with accordingly. So, nothing will happen to an 
innocent person. Moreover, it is not at all touching any original provisions. Out 
of the seven provisions, only certain explosive substances which are being 
used from Kashmir to Kanyakumari and everywhere are being dealt with by 
this Bill. In a short time, with less expenditure, they want to kill more people. 
So, this is the criminal scenario in the country. Therefore, to combat this kind 
of terrorism, these things have been included; otherwise, Sir, nothing is there 
in these provisions. There is no scope for including any extra provision in it. 
Whatever provisions and pr ocedures are required, they are already there. 
Only enhancement of punishment has been included in it. 
Sir, so far as the delegation of power to the magistrates is 
concerned, the Standing Committee has recommended this, since there are 
hundreds and thousands of cases. Ear lier, there were no cases. Every day, 
we hear about the use of this kind of explosive substances in Kashmir, 
Andhra, Bengal and so many other places. If, in each and every case, they 
require the permission of the Central Go vernment, the trial will be delayed. 
Therefore, the Committee has recommend ed for expediting the process. At 
the same time, it will be helpful to t he innocent persons and persons who are 
being tried in these cases. Therefore, the power has been delegated to the 
magistrates. There is nothing special in it. All safeguards are there in the court 
of faw and it will be done as per the regular procedure. 
Sir, one of the Members sugges ted amendment of the Indian 
Evidence Act and so many other things. All the valuable suggestions given by 
various Members have been noted down by me and those valuable 
suggestions would be used by my Ministry at an appropriate time. I request 
the hon. Members to kindly pass this Bill.
